s: What is the position of the State Legislature while an Article 249 resolution is in force?
o: may legislate only with the Rajya Sabha's consent
loses its power, which passes to the Governor
may still legislate, but the Parliamentary law prevails in a conflict
stands dissolved for the duration of the resolution
x: An Article 249 resolution does not suspend the State Legislature's power, but the Parliamentary law prevails if the two conflict.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 252?
o: Two or more State Legislatures must pass resolutions requesting parliamentary legislation
Any other State may adopt the law later by a resolution of its legislature
The requesting State Legislatures may independently repeal the law
Only Parliament can amend or repeal a law made under it
x: Only Parliament can amend or repeal a law enacted under Article 252; the requesting States cannot repeal it on their own.

s: How long does a law made for a State during President's Rule continue after the Proclamation ends?
o: the State Legislature alters, repeals or re-enacts it
the Supreme Court declares it permanent
the Governor issues an ordinance replacing it
x: Such a law does not automatically lapse when President’s Rule ends. It continues until the State Legislature alters, repeals or re-enacts it.

s: Under Article 252, resolutions passed by whom allow Parliament to legislate on a State List subject?
x: Article 252 needs resolutions of the legislatures of two or more States; one State is not enough.

s: Under which Article does Parliament exercise the legislative powers of a State Legislature during President's Rule?
x: Under Article 356 Parliament exercises the State Legislature's powers; Article 250 applies during a National Emergency and Article 252 on request of two or more States.

s: A law made by Parliament under Article 249 remains in force for what period after the Rajya Sabha resolution lapses?
x: A law under Article 249 ceases six months after the Rajya Sabha resolution lapses (each resolution lasts one year and can be renewed).

s: How long after a National Emergency ends does a law made by Parliament on a State List subject under Article 250 cease to have effect?
x: Laws made under Article 250 lapse six months after the Emergency ends.

s: Under Article 249, by what majority must a Rajya Sabha resolution authorising Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in the national interest be passed?
o: The unanimous vote of all Rajya Sabha members
A majority of members present and voting
At least two-thirds of the total membership of the Rajya Sabha
At least two-thirds of members present and voting
x: Under Article 249 the Rajya Sabha resolution needs two-thirds of the members present and voting — not two-thirds of total membership.

s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Article 249 – Rajya Sabha resolution in national interest
Article 356 – Proclamation of President's Rule in a State
Article 252 – Rajya Sabha resolution in national interest
x: Article 252 is triggered by a request of two or more State Legislatures; the Rajya Sabha resolution in national interest is Article 249.

s: Which one of the following is NOT an example of legislation enacted under Article 252?
o: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
x: The Prize Competition Act, 1955, the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 were enacted under Article 252 on resolutions of two or more States. The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is not an Article 252 law; it was enacted to implement an international (Stockholm) commitment, i.e. under Article 253.

s: Under which Article did Parliament enact the Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994?
x: It is an example of a law made by Parliament under Article 252 following resolutions by two or more State Legislatures.

s: Under Article 250, to which area may laws made by Parliament on State List subjects extend?
o: Only the State where the emergency originated
The whole or any part of India
x: Under Article 250, during a National Emergency, Parliament's laws on State subjects can extend to the whole or any part of India. 'Only consenting States' describes Article 252.

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 249:
1. The resolution is passed by the Rajya Sabha by two-thirds of members present and voting.
2. The resolution remains in force for up to one year and can be renewed.
3. The Lok Sabha must also pass a concurring resolution.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Article 249 needs only a Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds present and voting, valid up to one year and renewable; the Lok Sabha takes no part.

s: In which year was the Prize Competition Act, the first law in the Article 252 list, passed?
x: The Prize Competition Act, 1955 came first; the Wild Life Act (1972), Water Act (1974) and Urban Land Ceiling Act (1976) followed.

s: Under Article 253, whose consent does Parliament need to make a law on a State List subject to implement an international treaty?
o: The consent of all the States
The consent of a majority of the States
The consent of the States concerned
x: Article 253 lets Parliament implement treaties for the whole or any part of India without the consent of any State.

s: What does Article 253 of the Constitution deal with?
o: Legislation for giving effect to international agreements
Legislation for two or more States by consent
Legislation on the State List in the national interest
Repugnancy between Union and State laws
x: Article 253 empowers Parliament to make laws to implement international treaties, agreements and conventions.

s: Article 248 is located in which Part of the Constitution?
x: Article 248 is located in Part XI, which deals with relations between the Union and the States and extends from Articles 245 to 263.

s: What did the Sarkaria Commission recommend regarding residuary powers, apart from taxation?
o: Giving residuary taxation exclusively to the States
Moving all residuary powers except taxation to the Concurrent List
Transferring all residuary powers to the State List
x: The Sarkaria Commission in 1988 recommended moving all residuary powers other than taxation to the Concurrent List.

s:
Assertion (A): Residuary powers lie with the States in the United States of America and Australia.
Reason (R): Residuary powers lie with the Centre in Canada.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Canada giving residuary powers to the Centre says nothing about why the USA and Australia give them to the States.

s: Which of the following falls under Parliament's residuary power?
x: Space research, cyber law and residuary taxation are residuary subjects; police is State, education Concurrent and railways Union.

s: In Canada, with whom do residuary powers lie?
x: India and Canada vest residuary powers in the Centre; the USA and Australia vest them in the States.

s: With whom did residuary powers of legislation lie in the former State of Jammu and Kashmir until August 2019?
x: Under the former Article 370 arrangement, residuary powers in J&K lay with the State, not with Parliament as in other States.

s: In India, the residuary power of legislation is vested in Parliament by which combination?
o: Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List
Article 249 and Entry 97 of the State List
Article 250 and Entry 98 of the Concurrent List
Article 253 and Entry 97 of the Concurrent List
x: Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List together confer residuary legislative power on Parliament.

s: Article 246A was inserted by which Constitutional Amendment Act?
x: Article 246A was introduced by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, which established the constitutional framework for GST.

s: Which Article provides for the Inter-State Council?
x: Articles 256-263 deal with administrative relations, ending with Article 263 on the Inter-State Council.

s: What does Article 281 of the Constitution deal with?
x: Article 281 deals with the Finance Commission's recommendations; the Commission itself is constituted under Article 280.

s: From the constitution of which country was the scheme of distribution of legislative powers in the Indian Constitution borrowed?
x: India's scheme of legislative distribution follows the Canadian model.

s: In which Part of the Constitution is the freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse (Articles 301-307)?
x: Articles 301-307 form Part XIII; Part XI covers Union-State relations.

s: Which Articles make up Part XI (Relations between the Union and the States) of the Constitution?
x: Part XI covers Articles 245-263: legislative relations (245-255) and administrative relations (256-263).

s: Under Article 255, what is the status of an Act passed without the required previous sanction but later assented to by the Governor or President?
o: not invalid merely for want of that sanction
valid only if upheld by the Supreme Court
x: Article 255 treats the recommendation or previous sanction as procedural; subsequent assent prevents invalidity on that ground alone.

s: Which Article deals with repugnancy between Union and State laws?
x: Article 254 deals with repugnancy; Article 255 concerns recommendations and previous sanctions as procedural matters, and Article 248 with residuary powers.

s: Under which Article may Parliament set up additional courts for the better administration of Union laws?
x: Article 247 allows additional courts for Union laws; 248 is residuary power, 251 inconsistency and 255 procedure.

s: A State law on a State List subject conflicts with a valid Parliamentary law under the Concurrent List. Which ordinarily prevails?
o: The later of the two laws
The law approved by the Governor
x: The Concurrent List has precedence over the State List, so a valid Parliamentary law on a Concurrent matter ordinarily prevails over an inconsistent State law.

s: Under Article 246, who has legislative competence over the Concurrent List?
o: Parliament only during a National Emergency
x: Under Article 246, Parliament alone legislates on the Union List, States on the State List, and both on the Concurrent List.

s: Under Article 246(4), on matters in which Lists may Parliament legislate for areas not included in a State (Union Territories)?
o: The Union and Concurrent Lists only
x: Article 246(4) lets Parliament legislate for areas not included in a State on matters in all three Lists, not merely the Union List.

s: Which Article empowers both Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws on GST?
x: Article 246A, inserted by the 101st Amendment, 2016, gives Parliament and State Legislatures simultaneous power to make GST laws; only Parliament makes laws on inter-State supply.

s: The Union List and Concurrent List originally had 97 and 47 subjects. How many do they have today?
x: The Union List now has 98 subjects (97 originally) and the Concurrent List 52 (47 originally).

s: Which Constitutional Amendment omitted Entries 52 and 55 of the State List?
x: The 101st Amendment (GST) omitted State Entries 52 and 55; the 42nd omitted 11, 19, 20, 29 and the 7th omitted 36.

s: Over which List does Article 246(3) give State Legislatures exclusive power?
x: Under Article 246(3) States have exclusive power over List II, subject to clauses (1) and (2).

s: Under Article 246A, who alone can make GST laws on inter-State supply of goods and services?
x: Article 246A gives Parliament and States simultaneous GST power, but only Parliament legislates on inter-State supply (IGST).

s: Which Constitutional Amendment omitted Entry 36 of the State List?
x: Entry 36 went with the 7th Amendment (1956); entries 11, 19, 20 and 29 with the 42nd, and 52 and 55 with the 101st.

s: In which List does preventive detention for reasons connected with the security of a State and public order fall?
x: Concurrent List Entry 3 covers preventive detention for State security and public order, while Union List Entry 9 covers it for defence, foreign affairs and security of India.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Trade and commerce within a State — Union List
x: Agriculture is a State List subject, so B is correct. Trade and commerce within a State is a State List subject (not Union), while currency and foreign loans are Union List subjects (not State or Concurrent).

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about preservation of livestock (cow slaughter)?
o: Parliament can legislate on it through Articles 249, 250 or 252
Preservation of livestock is a State List subject
Article 48 is relevant to constitutional policy on preservation of livestock
Parliament may legislate on it only through the ordinary Union List power
x: Being a State subject, Parliament can legislate on it through routes such as Articles 249, 250 or 252, not through the ordinary Union List power.

s: Which of the following examples has been cited in debates concerning use of the Concurrent List to reach State subjects?
o: Farm Laws through Concurrent List Entry 33
Currency regulation through State List Entry 15
Foreign affairs through Concurrent List Entry 3
x: Farm Laws were discussed as an example of Concurrent List Entry 33 being used in a field associated with agriculture, which is State List Entry 14.

s: Which one of the following is the odd one out with reference to the Concurrent List in the Seventh Schedule?
x: Fisheries is a State List subject. Succession, criminal law and civil procedure are subjects in the Concurrent List.

s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Defence and armed forces – Union List
Space research – Residuary subject under Article 248
x: Education is a Concurrent List subject, not Union List. Defence is Union, public order is State (Entry 1), and space research is residuary under Article 248.

s: The constitutional basis for Parliament enacting the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act is primarily found in which entry?
x: Prevention of cruelty to animals is placed in Concurrent List Entry 17, enabling Parliament to enact central legislation on the subject.

s: In which List does adulteration of foodstuffs fall?
x: Adulteration of foodstuffs, drugs and electricity are Concurrent List subjects.

s: At which Entry of the State List are elections to the State Legislature placed?
x: State Entry 37 covers elections to the State Legislature; 45 is land revenue, 50 mineral-right taxes and 26 intra-State trade.

s: Which Constitutional Amendment moved forests from the State List to the Concurrent List?
x: The 42nd Amendment moved forests and education, among others, from the State List to the Concurrent List.

s: Under Article 243-C(1), who decides the composition of Panchayats?
x: Panchayats are a State subject (Entry 5), and Article 243-C(1) lets the State Legislature decide their composition.

s: In which List does preventive detention for reasons connected with defence, foreign affairs or the security of India fall?
x: This is Union List Entry 9; preventive detention for State security and public order is Concurrent Entry 3.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the territorial extent of laws?
o: Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of India
A parliamentary law is not invalid merely because it has extra-territorial operation
A State Legislature may ordinarily legislate for another State's territory without any territorial connection
A State law needs a sufficient territorial nexus for extra-territorial reach
x: A State law requires a sufficient territorial nexus for any extra-territorial reach, so the last statement is false.

s: Who makes regulations having the force of Acts of Parliament for the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep?
o: Chief Secretary of the Union Territory
x: Regulations made by the President for Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep have the force and effect of an Act of Parliament.

s: In Scheduled Areas, who may bar or modify the application of Acts of Parliament?
x: The Governor may bar or modify the application of Acts of Parliament in Scheduled Areas.

s: Who can make laws with extra-territorial operation?
x: Only Parliament can make extra-territorial laws (Article 245(2)); a State law needs a territorial nexus.

s: When may a State law reach outside the State?
x: A State legislature makes laws for its own State; outside reach is valid only with a real territorial nexus.

s: Articles 301 to 303 principally restrict Parliament from doing which of the following in relation to trade and commerce?
o: Making any law concerning inter-State trade
x: Articles 301 to 303 restrict discriminatory or preferential treatment between States in laws relating to trade and commerce.

s: Whose previous sanction does a State Bill imposing reasonable restrictions on inter-State trade in the public interest require?
x: A State may impose reasonable restrictions on inter-State trade in the public interest, but such a Bill needs the President's previous sanction.

s: The Supreme Court's advisory opinion of November 2025 was reported in connection with which issue?
o: Deemed assent and timelines for Governors and the President
Allocation of residuary powers to States
Transfer of forests to the Union List
x: The advisory opinion rejected deemed assent and fixed timelines concerning Governors and the President.

s: Under Article 251, which law prevails if a Parliamentary law made under Article 249 or 250 conflicts with a State law?
o: both laws become void to the extent of conflict
x: Article 251 provides that a Parliamentary law made under Article 249 or 250 prevails over an inconsistent State law.

s: Which of the following is INCORRECT about repugnancy on Concurrent List subjects?
o: Repugnancy is dealt with under Article 250.
In a conflict, the Central law generally prevails.
The Central-law rule has an exception relating to Presidential assent.
A reserved State law that gets Presidential assent may prevail under Article 254(2).
x: Repugnancy on Concurrent subjects is dealt with by Article 254, not Article 250 (Emergency legislation).

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 254(2)?
o: A repugnant State law on a Concurrent List subject prevails in that State if it receives the President's assent
The State law must be reserved for the consideration of the President
Parliament can later amend or repeal such a State law by a fresh law
Such a State law, once assented to, prevails throughout India
x: A State law assented to under Article 254(2) prevails only in that State, not throughout India.

s: The MMDR (Amendment) Bill, 2026 was reported as restricting the States' power to tax which subject?
x: The Bill was reported as restricting State taxation power over mineral rights and mineral-bearing land. Kerala viewed this as encroachment on State List Entries 18 and 50.

s: Kerala said the MMDR (Amendment) Bill, 2026 enters State List Entry 18 and which other Entry?
x: Kerala argued the Bill enters State Entry 18 (land) and Entry 50 (taxes on mineral rights).

s: Why do States mainly demand a review of Centre-State relations?
x: States seek a review of Centre-State relations because they lack adequate resources.

s: 'What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly' is the principle behind which doctrine?
x: This maxim underlies the doctrine of colourable legislation, which checks whether a legislature crosses its competence under a permissible guise.

s: Which case upheld a State prohibition law under the doctrine of pith and substance?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce
State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara
K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa
x: In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the prohibition law was upheld under pith and substance; its incidental encroachment did not change its true character.

s: Which doctrine requires legislative entries to be read together so that each can operate harmoniously?
x: Harmonious construction requires apparently overlapping entries to be interpreted together so that both retain operative effect.

s: What is the effect of the Doctrine of Severability?
o: The whole statute is declared void
Only the unconstitutional part is declared void, if separable
A law is tested only by its title
Parliament must re-enact the entire law
x: Under severability, only the unconstitutional part of a law is struck down if it can be separated; the rest survives.

s: Which doctrine holds that a pre-Constitution law that conflicts with a Fundamental Right stays dormant and revives if that right is amended?
x: Under the doctrine of eclipse such a law is not dead ab initio but only overshadowed, and it revives when the right is amended.

s: What does judicial review by the higher judiciary test the constitutional validity of?
o: Both legislative acts and executive actions
x: Judicial review is the higher judiciary's power to test both laws and executive action.

s: Which doctrine looks at the true nature of a law and ignores its incidental encroachment on another List?
x: The doctrine of pith and substance resolves overlaps between the Lists by examining the law's true nature.

s: The Doctrine of Eclipse is associated with which case?
o: Prafulla Kumar v Bank of Commerce
Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v State of M.P.
Kameshwar Singh v State of Bihar
A.K. Gopalan v State of Madras
x: The Doctrine of Eclipse comes from Bhikaji Narain Dhakras; Prafulla Kumar is a pith and substance case.

s: With which doctrine is K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v State of Orissa (1953) linked?
x: Gajapati Narayan Deo and Kameshwar Singh are colourable legislation cases: what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.

s: In which case did the Privy Council apply the doctrine of pith and substance in 1947?
o: State of Bombay v F.N. Balsara
Kameshwar Singh v State of Bihar
Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v Bank of Commerce
Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v State of M.P.
x: Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v Bank of Commerce (1947) is the Privy Council case on pith and substance.

s: With which case is the origin of judicial review associated?
x: Judicial review traces to Marbury v Madison (1803) in the USA.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the executive power of the Union?
o: The President's power as Supreme Commander is not subject to regulation by law
It may be exercised through subordinate officers
It may be exercised directly by the President
The President is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces
x: The President's power as Supreme Commander of the armed forces is regulated by law.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Real executive – Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister
Head of the Council of Ministers – President
x: The President is only the nominal or constitutional head; real executive power lies with the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The President holds Rank 1 in the Order of Precedence.
2. The President is the Head of the State, not the Head of the Government.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
x: The President is first in the Order of Precedence and is Head of State, while the Prime Minister heads the Government.

s: Under Article 53(2), what is true of the President's supreme command of the Defence Forces?
x: Article 53(2) makes the President Supreme Commander of the armed forces, but its exercise is regulated by law.

s: Under Article 77, in whose name is all executive action of the Government of India taken?
x: Article 77 says all executive action of the Government of India is taken in the name of the President.

s: Under which Article is the President a part of Parliament?
x: Article 79 says Parliament consists of the President and the two Houses.

s: Who ordinarily exercises executive power in a Union Territory?
o: Chief Secretary of the Union Territory
Union Home Minister in every matter
Lieutenant Governor or Administrator, as the President's representative
x: The Lieutenant Governor or Administrator exercises executive power in a Union Territory as the President's representative.

s: Which Constitutional Amendment inserted Article 239AA, giving Delhi a Legislative Assembly and a Council of Ministers?
x: The 69th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991 inserted Article 239AA.

s: On what is the model proposed for safeguarding Ladakh's interests based?
o: Article 371-like safeguards instead of the Sixth Schedule
x: The proposed model for Ladakh is based on safeguards similar to those under Article 371, rather than the Sixth Schedule.

s: Under Article 239, through whom does the President administer Union Territories?
o: The Governor of a neighbouring State
x: Article 239 runs UTs through the President acting via an Administrator or Lieutenant Governor.

s: Who became the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi in March 2026?
x: Former US ambassador Taranjit Singh Sandhu replaced V.K. Saxena as Delhi LG in March 2026; Saxena moved to Ladakh.

s: Who was the Lieutenant Governor of Puducherry from 2016 to 2021?
x: Kiran Bedi, India's first woman IPS officer, was LG of Puducherry from May 2016 to February 2021.

s: Under Article 239AA, which of the following is NOT excluded from the Delhi Legislative Assembly's competence?
x: Public order, police and land are outside the Delhi Assembly's competence under Article 239AA; public health is not among the exclusions.

s: How does Article 258(2) differ from Article 258(1)?
o: It applies only during a National Emergency
It concerns inter-State agreements on river-valley projects
It lets Parliament by law confer duties on State officers without State consent
It lets the Governor transfer State functions to the Union
x: Under Article 258(2), Parliament may by law confer powers or duties on State officers without State consent; Article 258(1) involves Presidential entrustment with State consent.

s: Under which Article may a State's failure to comply with Union directions be treated as a breakdown of constitutional machinery?
x: Article 365 allows such non-compliance to be treated as a breakdown of constitutional machinery, opening the way to action under Article 356.

s: What does Article 258A of the Constitution deal with?
o: Agreements between States on river valley projects
Power of a State, with the consent of the Union Government, to entrust its functions to the Union
Entrustment of Union functions to States by Parliament without State consent
Directions of the Union to States during a Financial Emergency
x: Article 258A lets a State entrust its functions to the Union (APPSC-GS 2023). Calling it 'agreements between States on river valley projects' is a known wrong statement. Entrustment by Parliament without consent is Article 258(2), and Financial Emergency directions fall under Article 360.

s: Under Article 258A, with whose consent may a State entrust its functions to the Union?
x: Article 258A lets a State entrust functions to the Union with the Union's consent (asked in APPSC GS 2023).

s: In whom does Article 154 of the Constitution vest the executive power of a State?
x: Article 154 vests the executive power of the State in the Governor, who may exercise it directly or through subordinate officers.

s: Under Article 73, the executive power of the Union extends to matters on which body can make laws?
x: Article 73 extends Union executive power to matters on which Parliament can legislate and to rights and authority under treaties or agreements.

s: To which matters does the executive power of a State under Article 162 ordinarily extend?
o: State Legislature can legislate within the territory of the State
Union Parliament can legislate throughout India
x: Article 162 extends State executive power to matters on which the State Legislature has power to make laws, within the State's territory.

s: In relation to remission under Article 161, whose advice has the Supreme Court held the Governor is bound by?
x: The Governor must act on the advice of the State Cabinet while exercising the remission power under Article 161.

s: The Constitution provides special responsibility for law and order to the Governors of which States?
x: The Governor of Nagaland has special responsibility under Article 371A, and the Governor of Arunachal Pradesh under Article 371H, in relation to law and order.

s: Under Article 163(1), in which matters does the Council of Ministers NOT aid and advise the Governor?
x: Article 163(1) excludes the Governor's discretionary matters from the Council of Ministers' advice; remission under Article 161 follows Cabinet advice.

s: With whom does executive power over Concurrent List subjects ordinarily rest?
o: the States, subject to constitutional or statutory exceptions
x: By default, executive power over Concurrent subjects stays with the States; the Centre exercises it only where the Constitution or a Parliamentary law expressly provides.

s: The rule on executive power over Concurrent List subjects is found in the provisos to which Articles?
x: The provisos to Articles 73 and 162 keep Concurrent executive power with the States unless the Constitution or a Parliamentary law gives it to the Centre.

s:
Consider the following statements about executive power in Concurrent List subjects:
1. By default it rests with the States.
2. The Centre executes such a subject only where the Constitution or a Parliamentary law expressly provides.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: the default lies with the States, and the Centre executes only where the Constitution or a law of Parliament expressly says so.

s: Under Article 356, the powers of which of the following remain untouched when President's Rule is imposed in a State?
x: Article 356 expressly leaves the powers of the State High Court untouched; the President takes over the executive and the Council of Ministers is dismissed.

s: Under Article 353, what is the effect of a National Emergency on executive relations?
o: State governments are suspended and replaced by administrators
The Union may direct States on any matter, but State governments are not suspended
The State Council of Ministers is dismissed in every State
The powers of the High Courts pass to the Union executive
x: During a National Emergency the Union's power of direction expands under Article 353, but State governments continue and are not suspended.

s: Which of the following is a possible effect of a Financial Emergency under Article 360?
o: The Union automatically assumes all State legislative powers
State Money and Financial Bills may be reserved for the President
x: During a Financial Emergency, the Centre may require Money Bills and other Financial Bills of States to be reserved for the President's consideration.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about emergencies and Union-State executive relations?
o: In a National Emergency the Union may direct any State on any matter
In a National Emergency State governments are suspended
Under Article 356 the State Council of Ministers is dismissed
Under Article 360 the salaries of State employees may be cut
x: A National Emergency lets the Union direct States on any matter, but State governments are not suspended.

s: Which emergency has never been used in India so far?
x: The Financial Emergency under Article 360 is the only emergency never used so far.

s: How do All India Services differ from Central Services?
o: Common to the Union and the States
Recruited only by State Public Service Commissions
x: All India Services are common to the Union and the States, while Central Services relate to Union subjects only.

s: Under Article 312, Parliament may create a new All India Service when the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by what majority?
o: A majority of the members present and voting
A simple majority of the total membership
Two-thirds of the members present and voting
x: Article 312 requires a Rajya Sabha resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting before Parliament can create a new All India Service.

s: Which one of the following services is specifically mentioned in Article 312 as capable of being created as an All India Service?
x: Article 312 expressly includes the possibility of creating an All India Judicial Service.

s: Which body recruits officers of the All India Services on an all-India basis?
x: UPSC recruits them; the Centre trains them and they serve in State cadres.

s: Who described the All India Services as the 'Steel Frame' of India?
x: Sardar Patel championed the All India Services and called them the 'Steel Frame' of India.

s: Why are All India Services sometimes criticised from the federal perspective?
o: Their officers are governed by Central rules and States lack full control over them.
They are confined entirely to local government administration.
They are recruited exclusively by State Public Service Commissions.
They have no connection with the Union Government.
x: The federal criticism is that Central rules govern the officers and States do not exercise full control over them, thereby restricting State autonomy.

s: The proposed amendments to the All India Services (Cadre) Rules, 1954 were associated with which issue?
o: Compulsory retirement of all AIS officers by State Governments
Central deputation without the consent of the State or the officer
Replacement of UPSC recruitment by direct State recruitment
Abolition of State cadres for All India Services
x: The proposed amendments would enable the Centre to order central deputation without the consent of the State Government or the officer, with the Centre's order becoming final after a prescribed time.

s: Which of the following is a Central Service and NOT an All India Service?
x: The Indian Foreign Service (IFS) is a Central Service; the Indian Forest Service (IFoS), IAS and IPS are All India Services.

s: Which Act governs the All India Services?
x: The existing All India Services are governed by the All India Services Act, 1951.

s: On whose recommendation does the President appoint officers of the All India Services?
x: AIS officers are recruited by the UPSC and appointed by the President on its recommendation.

s:
Consider the following statements about officers of the All India Services:
1. They are appointed by the President.
2. They can be dismissed by the State Government under which they are serving.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: AIS officers are appointed by the President, and only the Union Government can dismiss or remove them, even when they serve a State.

s: Who can dismiss or remove an IPS officer serving in a State cadre?
x: Like all All India Service officers, an IPS officer can be dismissed or removed only by the Union Government.

s: In which year was the Indian Forest Service, an All India Service, created?
x: The Indian Forest Service was created in 1966; it is an All India Service along with the IAS and IPS.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Sarkaria Commission?
o: It recommended a temporary Inter-State Council convened only during emergencies
It was set up in June 1983 under Justice R.S. Sarkaria
It recommended that Article 356 be used sparingly
x: The Sarkaria Commission recommended a permanent Inter-State Council, not a temporary one.

s: Who first chaired the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966)?
x: The ARC was chaired by Morarji Desai and then K. Hanumanthaiya; M.C. Setalvad led its study team.

s: The Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State relations made how many recommendations?
x: The Sarkaria Commission (June 1983) made 247 recommendations, including a permanent Inter-State Council.

s: Who succeeded Morarji Desai as chairman of the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966)?
x: Morarji Desai first chaired the ARC; K. Hanumanthaiya took over after him. M.C. Setalvad led its study team on Centre-State relations.

s: On whose recommendation was the Inter-State Council set up in 1990?
x: The Council was set up on 28 May 1990 by Presidential order on the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Inter-State Council:
1. It is chaired by the Prime Minister.
2. It decides by consensus.
3. Its recommendations are binding on the Union and the States.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Council is chaired by the PM and works by consensus, but its recommendations are not binding.

s: Who chairs the Standing Committee of the Inter-State Council?
x: The Council itself is chaired by the PM, but its Standing Committee is chaired by the Union Home Minister.

s: Who establishes the Inter-State Council under Article 263?
x: Article 263 is an enabling provision: the President sets up the Council by order, as done on 28 May 1990.

s: How many Union Cabinet Ministers, nominated by the Prime Minister, are members of the Inter-State Council?
x: The Council has the PM as chairman, all Chief Ministers, UT heads and six Union Cabinet Ministers nominated by the PM.

s: Under which Act is the Apex Council for disputes arising from the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh provided?
x: For bifurcation disputes, the Inter-State Council and the Apex Council under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 were suggested.

s: What did the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966) recommend the establishment of?
x: The ARC urged an Inter-State Council and non-partisan Governors.

s: Which Article requires that the executive power of every State be exercised so as to ensure compliance with the laws made by Parliament?
x: Article 256 requires State executive power to ensure compliance with laws made by Parliament and permits the Union to issue directions for that purpose.

s: If a State fails to comply with Union directions, which Article lets the President hold that its government cannot be carried on per the Constitution?
x: Article 365 lets the President draw that conclusion when a State fails to comply with Union directions, which can open the way to action under Article 356.

s: Under Article 257, on which matter may the Union issue directions to a State?
o: Protection of railways within the State
x: Article 257 directions cover means of communication of national or military importance and protection of railways; public order is not among them.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 258(2) – State entrusts its functions to the Union with the Centre's consent
Article 258(1) – President entrusts Union functions to a State with the State's consent
Article 258A – Parliament confers duties on State officers by law without State consent
Article 258(1) – Parliament confers duties on State officers by law without State consent
x: Article 258(1) is Presidential entrustment of Union functions to a State with its consent; 258(2) is entrustment by Parliamentary law without consent; 258A is State-to-Union entrustment with the Centre's consent.

s:
Consider the following statements about delegation of functions:
1. Under Article 258(2), Parliament may entrust functions to a State without its consent.
2. Under Article 258A, the Governor entrusts State functions to the Union with the Centre's consent.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: 258(2) needs no State consent, and under 258A the Governor entrusts functions to the Union with the Centre's consent.

s: Under Article 258(1), by whom are functions of the Union entrusted to a State?
o: Parliament by law, without the State's consent
The Governor, with the Centre's consent
The President, with the State's consent
The Union Home Minister, without consent
x: Article 258(1) lets the President entrust Union functions to a State with the State's consent; 258(2) is Parliament by law without consent.

s: Article 258A was inserted by which Constitutional Amendment Act?
x: Article 258A was inserted by the Seventh Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956.

s: In what capacity do Chief Secretaries attend Zonal Council meetings?
x: Advisers such as Chief Secretaries attend Zonal Councils without voting rights; each State is represented by its Chief Minister and two Ministers.

s: Which of the following is NOT one of the five Zonal Councils established under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956?
x: The five councils are Northern, Central, Eastern, Western and Southern. The North-Eastern Council was created separately under the North-Eastern Council Act, 1971.

s: What kind of bodies are Zonal Councils?
o: statutory advisory bodies whose recommendations are not binding
executive bodies that allocate State finances
constitutional bodies that can dissolve State Legislatures
judicial bodies whose decisions bind the States
x: Zonal Councils are statutory, deliberative and advisory bodies; their recommendations do not bind the States.

s: Which one of the following is correct about the chairmanship of the Zonal Councils?
o: The Chief Minister of the largest State chairs each council permanently
The President chairs them; the Union Home Minister is vice-chairman
The Union Home Minister chairs all five; vice-chairmanship rotates annually among member Chief Ministers
The Prime Minister chairs them; Governors are permanent vice-chairpersons
x: The Union Home Minister is the common Chairman of all five Zonal Councils, and the vice-chairmanship rotates annually among the Chief Ministers of member States.

s: Which one of the following is NOT a member of the Southern Zonal Council?
x: The Southern Zonal Council comprises Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala, Telangana and the UT of Puducherry. Telangana (often left out of older tables) and Puducherry are members, as is Kerala; Goa is not among the members.

s: Into how many States and Union Territories did the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 reorganise India?
x: The States Reorganisation Act, passed in November 1956, created 14 States and 6 Union Territories. The other combinations are incorrect. The same Act set up the five Zonal Councils in its Part III.

s: Under which law was the North-Eastern Council set up?
x: The NEC rests on a separate NEC Act, 1971, while Zonal Councils come from the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

s:
Consider the following statements about the North-Eastern Council:
1. Sikkim was added to it in 2002.
2. Since 2018 the Union Home Minister is its ex-officio chairman.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: Sikkim joined the NEC in 2002, and since 2018 the Union Home Minister is its ex-officio chairman.

s: Who is the vice-chairman of a Zonal Council?
o: The Chief Minister of a member State, by annual rotation
The senior-most Governor of the zone
The Chief Secretary of the host State
x: The Union Home Minister chairs all Zonal Councils; Chief Ministers of member States serve as vice-chairman by annual rotation.

s: Who proposed the setting up of Zonal Councils in 1956?
x: Jawaharlal Nehru proposed the Zonal Councils, which were set up under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

s: Near which place was the 31st meeting of the Southern Zonal Council held in August 2026?
x: The 31st Southern Zonal Council met on 20 August 2026 near Mamallapuram, chaired by Union Home Minister Amit Shah.

s: Besides the Chief Minister, how many other ministers of each member State are members of a Zonal Council?
x: Each State is represented by its Chief Minister and two other ministers.

s: In which year did the Union Public Service Commission replace the Federal Public Service Commission?
x: The UPSC replaced the Federal Public Service Commission in 1950, when the Constitution came into force.

s: In discharging its duty under Article 355, on what condition may the Union deploy armed or central forces in a State?
o: only with the State Government's consent
with or without the State's consent
only when the State Legislature authorises it
only after a National Emergency is proclaimed
x: The Union may deploy armed or central forces with or without State consent in discharge of its Article 355 duty.

s: What is the constitutional basis for the Union's deployment of armed or central forces in States?
o: Entry 2A of the Union List, inserted through the 42nd Constitutional Amendment
Entry 97 of the Concurrent List, inserted through the First Amendment
Entry 1 of the State List, inserted through the Seventh Amendment
Entry 2 of the State List, inserted through the 44th Amendment
x: Entry 2A of the Union List, associated with the 42nd Constitutional Amendment, provides the relevant Union List basis for deployment.

s: Why do States object to Union deployment of armed or central forces without their consent?
o: Public order and police are Union List subjects
Police is a Concurrent List subject
Public order and police are State List subjects
Defence is a State List subject
x: Public order and police are Entries 1 and 2 of the State List, so deployment without consent touches State authority.

s: By what is a Joint State Public Service Commission created, and who appoints its members?
o: an Act of Parliament; the President
a State law; the Chief Ministers concerned
the UPSC; the Union Home Minister
x: A Joint State Public Service Commission is created by an Act of Parliament, and its members are appointed by the President.

s: Article 323A, inserted by which Constitutional Amendment, deals with administrative tribunals for the Union and the States?
x: Article 323A was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, to provide for administrative tribunals.

s: Under Article 315, when can a Joint State Public Service Commission for two or more States be set up?
x: Article 315 allows a JSPSC for two or more States if their legislatures pass resolutions; Parliament then creates it by law.

s: Article 261 of the Constitution provides for which of the following?
o: Uniformity of service conditions in All-India Services
Distribution of financial resources between the Union and the States
Full faith and credit throughout India to public acts, records and judicial proceedings
Adjudication of inter-State river water disputes
x: Article 261 requires full faith and credit throughout India to public acts, records and judicial proceedings of the Union and every State.

s: With which purpose are grants under Article 275 specifically associated?
o: discretionary grants for any public purpose
compensation to States for GST revenue loss
Scheduled Tribe welfare and administration of Scheduled Areas
x: Article 275 provides grants for the welfare of Scheduled Tribes and the administration of Scheduled Areas; discretionary grants for any public purpose fall under Article 282.

s: With which subject is the authority that may be established under Article 307 associated?
x: Article 307 provides for an authority to carry out the purposes of the constitutional provisions relating to trade, commerce and intercourse within India.

s: Which one of the following extra-constitutional devices of Centre-State cooperation is presided over by the President?
x: The Governors' Conference is presided over by the President. The Chief Ministers' Conference is presided over by the Prime Minister; the Chief Secretaries' Conference and the Central Council for Local Government are other extra-constitutional devices not chaired by the President.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Water tribunals are statutory (ISRWD Act, 1956); Zonal Councils are statutory, the ISC is constitutional and the NDC is extra-constitutional.

s: Who presides over the Chief Ministers' Conference?
x: The CMs' Conference is chaired by the Prime Minister, while the Governors' Conference is chaired by the President.

s: Under which Article are grants for any public purpose given at the Union's discretion?
x: Article 282 provides discretionary grants; Article 275 grants are linked to ST welfare and Scheduled Areas.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about inter-State water disputes?
o: The Mullaperiyar dam is located on the Godavari river
The Mahanadi dispute is between Odisha and Chhattisgarh
The Mullaperiyar dam is situated in Kerala
The Mullaperiyar dam is operated by Tamil Nadu under a lease
x: Mullaperiyar is on the Periyar, not the Godavari.

s: Andhra Pradesh is included in which Zonal Council and is party to which combination of water tribunals?
o: Southern Zonal Council; Godavari, Krishna and Vansadhara
Eastern Zonal Council; Narmada, Cauvery and Ravi-Beas
Southern Zonal Council; Ravi-Beas, Cauvery and Mahadayi
Central Zonal Council; Godavari, Narmada and Mahadayi
x: Andhra Pradesh belongs to the Southern Zonal Council and is party to the Godavari, Krishna and Vansadhara water dispute tribunals.

s: The Vansadhara Water Disputes Tribunal (2010) concerns a dispute between Andhra Pradesh and which State?
x: The Vansadhara Tribunal, constituted on 24 February 2010, deals with the AP-Odisha dispute.

s: Under Article 262, Parliament enacted which law for adjudicating inter-State river disputes?
x: Article 262 led to the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, under which water tribunals are set up.

s: On which river does the Mullaperiyar dam, operated by Tamil Nadu, stand?
x: The Mullaperiyar dam (1895) is on the Periyar in Kerala and is operated by Tamil Nadu.

s: Who headed the first Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal constituted in 1969?
x: Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal-I (1969) was headed by Justice R.S. Bachawat.

s: In which year was the Godavari Water Disputes Tribunal constituted?
x: The Godavari tribunal was set up in 1969 and gave its award in 1980.

s: In which year was the second Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal (Krishna-II) constituted?
x: Krishna-II was constituted in 2004 and reported on 30 December 2010; Krishna-I under R.S. Bachawat was set up in 1969.

s: Which Article of the Constitution empowers the States to levy tax on professions, trades, callings and employments?
x: Article 276 deals with profession tax; the ceiling is Rs 2,500 per person per year.

s: Which of the following sets contains only taxes or levies associated with the State domain?
o: Land revenue, agricultural income tax, State excise on alcohol and taxes on vehicles
Customs duty, corporation tax, Union excise duty and income tax
Goods and Services Tax, customs duty, wealth tax and corporation tax
Surcharge on Union taxes, customs duty, export duty and corporation tax
x: Land revenue, agricultural income tax, State excise on alcohol and taxes on vehicles are included among taxes associated with the State domain. The other sets consist predominantly of Union taxes.

s: Under Article 268 (e.g. stamp duties on specified instruments), how are duties levied, collected and appropriated?
o: Levied, collected and appropriated exclusively by the Union
Levied and collected by the States but appropriated by the Union
Levied by the States and collected jointly by the Union and the States
Levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States
x: Article 268 covers duties levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States.

s: Under Article 269, how are taxes on the inter-State sale or purchase of goods (other than newspapers) levied and shared?
o: Levied and collected by the States and appropriated by them
Levied and collected by the Union but assigned to the States
Levied, collected and appropriated exclusively by the Union
Levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States
x: Under Article 269 the Union levies and collects these taxes (including taxes on consignment of goods) and assigns them to the States.

s: What happens to the proceeds of a surcharge levied on a tax covered by Article 270?
o: automatically divided between the Union and States
collected and kept by the State concerned
distributed on the GST Council's recommendation
x: Under Article 271, surcharges on Article 269 and 270 taxes are for Union purposes and are not shared with the States.

s: Which of the following is correctly matched?
o: Article 269 — Surcharge exclusively for the Union
Article 270 — Stamp duties collected and appropriated by States
x: Article 269A concerns IGST on inter-State supplies. Article 268 covers specified stamp duties, Article 269 covers assigned taxes, and Article 271 covers surcharges.

s: Since which Constitutional Amendment has corporation tax, levied and collected by the Union, been shared with the States?
x: Since the 80th Constitutional Amendment, corporation tax is part of the shareable pool of Union taxes.

s: Which taxes does Article 270 cover?
o: all Union List taxes without exception
only customs duties and Union excise duties
all State List taxes collected by the Union
Union taxes shared via the Finance Commission, excluding specified taxes, surcharges and cesses
x: Article 270 covers Union List taxes shared as recommended by the Finance Commission, excluding Article 268, 269 and 269A taxes, Article 271 surcharges and cesses.

s: Service tax was associated with Article 268A before that Article was omitted by which Constitutional Amendment?
x: Article 268A was introduced for service tax by the 88th Amendment in 2003 and was omitted by the 101st Amendment in 2016 with the introduction of GST.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the authority that levies it?
x: Excise on liquor is a State tax. Customs duty is levied by the Union, agricultural income tax by the States, and entertainment tax is largely subsumed in GST except for local bodies.

s: What is true of the proceeds of taxes under Article 269 that are assigned to the States?
o: Do not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India
Are shared on the GST Council's advice
Are kept by the Union as surcharges
Form part of the divisible pool under Article 270
x: Article 269 taxes are collected by the Union and assigned to the States, and their proceeds do not form part of the CFI.

s: Which of the following is NOT a tax levied only by the States?
x: Corporation tax is levied by the Union, never by the States; land revenue, agricultural income tax and liquor excise are State taxes.

s: Which one of the following was NOT folded into the Article 270 pool by the 80th Constitutional Amendment?
o: Taxes on stock-exchange transactions other than stamp duty
x: Pre-2000 taxes on stock-exchange transactions, estate duty, railway fares and newspapers were folded into the Article 270 pool. Surcharges remain exclusively for the Union under Article 271.

s: On whose advice are the proceeds of IGST on inter-State supply apportioned between the Centre and the States?
o: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
x: Article 269A provides for apportionment of IGST on inter-State supply between the Centre and the States on the advice of the GST Council.

s: Which Article of the Constitution concerns the Integrated GST (IGST)?
x: Article 269A, added by the 101st Amendment, deals with IGST; Article 270 covers taxes shared between the Centre and the States.

s: The Finance Commission is a quasi-judicial constitutional body established under which Article of the Constitution?
x: The Finance Commission is a quasi-judicial constitutional body under Article 280, in Part XII. Article 275 deals with grants and 282 with discretionary grants.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Sixteenth Finance Commission?
o: It retained the vertical share of States in the divisible pool at 41%
The Union Government accepted this recommendation in Budget 2026–27
Vertical share refers to distribution of the divisible pool among individual States
Distribution of the divisible pool among individual States is inter se devolution
x: Vertical devolution concerns the Centre–State share; distribution among individual States is inter se (horizontal) devolution.

s: The Fifteenth Finance Commission recommended what share of the divisible pool for the States?
x: The Fifteenth Finance Commission recommended 41 percent; 42 percent was the Fourteenth Finance Commission's figure.

s: What did the 2024 'Chalo Delhi' protest by southern States mainly oppose?
o: the replacement of grants by cesses
the abolition of State Development Loans
conditionality attached to Centrally Sponsored Schemes only
x: The protest concerned the perceived adverse effect of population-heavy or population-based criteria on the devolution share of southern States.

s: What does horizontal devolution of the divisible pool refer to?
o: Between the Centre and the States
Between the States and local bodies
x: Vertical devolution is the Centre-State share; horizontal devolution is distribution among the States, both recommended by the Finance Commission.

s: Under which Article does the Finance Commission recommend both vertical and horizontal devolution?
x: Article 280(3) tasks the Finance Commission with both the Centre-State share and its distribution among States.

s: Because cesses and surcharges stay outside the divisible pool, what is the effective devolution to States?
x: Cesses and surcharges, about 18% of gross tax revenue, stay outside the pool, so effective devolution is near 31-32% against the 41% award.

s: Which one of the following is associated with the recommendations of the Sixteenth Finance Commission regarding State finances?
o: A fiscal deficit ceiling of 3% of GDP for the Union alone
A fiscal deficit ceiling of 5% of GSDP and expansion of off-budget borrowing
A fiscal deficit ceiling of 3% of GSDP and ending off-budget borrowing
A prohibition on all State borrowing from domestic sources
x: The Sixteenth Finance Commission caps the State fiscal deficit at 3% of GSDP and calls for ending off-budget borrowing.

s: Which Finance Commission raised the States' share to 42% with a compositional shift towards unconditional transfers?
x: The Fourteenth FC gave 42% with more devolution and fewer grants, making transfers more unconditional (APPSC-G1 2017).

s: What was the tax devolution to the States in 2024-25?
x: Tax devolution in 2024-25 was Rs 12.87 lakh crore against a Budget Estimate of Rs 12.47 lakh crore.

s: What is the main effect on the States of a shift from grants to tax devolution?
o: More untied funds and greater fiscal autonomy for the States
More conditional transfers tied to central schemes
A fall in the States' share of central taxes
Higher matching shares for Centrally Sponsored Schemes
x: Devolution is formula-based and untied, so a shift from grants to devolution gives States more unconditional money and autonomy.

s: Who certifies the net proceeds relevant to the divisible pool?
o: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
x: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India certifies the net proceeds used in determining the divisible pool.

s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Article 265 – No tax except by authority of law
Article 266 – Consolidated Funds and Public Accounts
Article 268 – Contingency Fund of a State
x: Article 268 deals with duties levied by the Union but collected by the States; Contingency Funds are under Article 267.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Article 267 covers the Contingency Fund. Article 148 is the CAG, Article 266 the Consolidated Fund and Article 269A IGST.

s: Which Article exempts the property of the Union from taxation by the States?
x: Article 285 exempts Union property from State taxes; Article 289 exempts State property from Union taxes.

s: Which Article provides for the Consolidated Funds and Public Accounts of India and of the States?
x: Article 266 provides for the Consolidated Funds and Public Accounts; Article 267 is about Contingency Funds.

s: Which Article exempts the property of the States from Union taxation?
x: Article 289 exempts State property from Union taxes, though the Centre can tax a State's commercial operations.

s: Which Part of the Constitution deals with Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits?
x: Part XII (Articles 264-293) deals with Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits.

s: Into which fund are all revenues received by the Union, the loans raised by it and repayments of its loans credited?
x: Under Article 266, all Union revenues, loans raised and loan repayments go into the Consolidated Fund of India.

s: Which Article of the Constitution provides for the GST Council?
x: Article 279A, inserted by the 101st Amendment, provides for the GST Council.

s: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 inserted which set of provisions in connection with GST?
x: The 101st Amendment inserted Articles 246A, 269A and 279A for the GST framework and the GST Council.

s: Goods and Services Tax (GST) was introduced in India with effect from which date?
x: GST came into effect on 1 July 2017 pursuant to the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016.

s: Under Article 246A, who has the exclusive power to make GST laws on inter-State supplies?
x: Article 246A gives concurrent GST power to Parliament and State Legislatures, but Parliament alone legislates on inter-State supplies.

s: Who are the members of the GST Council?
o: the Union Home Minister, State Home Ministers and the RBI Governor
the Finance Commission Chairman and State Chief Secretaries
the Union Finance Minister, Union Minister of State for Finance and State Finance Ministers
the Prime Minister, Union Finance Minister and all Chief Ministers
x: The GST Council comprises the Union Finance Minister (Chairperson), the Union Minister of State in charge of Finance and the State Finance Ministers.

s: On which principle is the Goods and Services Tax (GST) based?
x: GST is a destination-based tax that subsumed about 17 earlier taxes.

s: Why can neither the Union nor the States alone carry a decision in the GST Council?
o: Because the Union Finance Minister does not vote in the Council
Because the States have a veto over all GST matters
Because the Council requires unanimous approval in every matter
Because the Centre has one-third and the States together have two-thirds of the weighted votes, while three-fourths is required
x: A GST Council decision needs three-fourths of the weighted votes. The Centre holds only one-third and all States together only two-thirds, so neither side can reach three-fourths alone; options A-C misstate the voting rules.

s: What did the Supreme Court hold in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022) about the recommendations of the GST Council?
o: Binding only when supported by a unanimous vote
Binding on Parliament and State Legislatures in every matter
Persuasive and not binding on Parliament and State Legislatures
x: The Court held that GST Council recommendations have persuasive value but are not binding on Parliament or State Legislatures.

s: Compensation Cess under the GST system was primarily imposed on which category of goods?
x: Compensation Cess on luxury and sin goods was used to fund compensation to States for GST-related revenue loss.

s: For how many years was GST compensation to the States guaranteed?
x: Compensation cess paid for States' GST revenue loss, guaranteed for 5 years (2017-22).

s: Under Article 269A, to which State does IGST revenue go?
x: GST is destination-based; under Article 269A IGST revenue goes to the destination State.

s: What weight does the vote of the Centre carry in the GST Council?
x: The Centre has one-third and all States together two-thirds of the weighted votes; decisions need three-fourths.

s: Which Constitution Amendment Bill became the 101st Amendment Act on GST?
x: The Constitution (122nd Amendment) Bill was enacted as the 101st Amendment Act, 2016.

s: Who is the chairperson of the GST Council?
o: Governor of the Reserve Bank of India
x: Under Article 279A, the Union Finance Minister chairs the GST Council.

s: What share of the weighted votes is needed for a decision of the GST Council?
x: Decisions need 3/4 of weighted votes; the Centre has 1/3 and the States together 2/3, so neither side can decide alone.

s: About how many taxes were replaced by the Goods and Services Tax?
x: GST, in force from 1 July 2017, replaced about 17 indirect taxes.

s: From when did 'GST 2.0' take effect?
x: GST began on 1 July 2017; GST 2.0 took effect in September 2025.

s: What is the post-2014 demand of Andhra Pradesh in the context of Centre-State relations?
o: separate representation in the Finance Commission
transfer of all Union taxes to the State
x: Andhra Pradesh has continued its post-2014 demand for special category status.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about grants-in-aid?
o: Statutory grants under Article 275 are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
Statutory grants are made on the recommendation of NITI Aayog
Discretionary grants under Article 282 may be made for any public purpose
Statutory grants are made on the recommendation of the Finance Commission
x: Statutory grants under Article 275 are made on the recommendation of the Finance Commission, not NITI Aayog.

s: Which of the following is true of discretionary grants under Article 282?
o: are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
may be made for any public purpose
are meant only for Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Areas
x: Article 282 permits discretionary grants for any public purpose; historically they were largely routed through the Planning Commission and are not charged on the Consolidated Fund.

s:
Consider the following statements about grants-in-aid:
1. Statutory grants under Article 275 are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
2. Discretionary grants under Article 282 are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Article 275 grants are charged on the CFI; Article 282 discretionary grants are not.

s: On whose recommendation are statutory grants-in-aid under Article 275 given?
x: Article 275 statutory grants are recommended by the Finance Commission, not NITI Aayog (APPSC-GS 2019).

s: Which of the following was NOT a parameter traditionally associated with special category status?
o: Strategic location along an international border
High per-capita income and commercially viable State finances
Low population density or a sizeable tribal population
x: Special category parameters included difficult terrain, low population density or sizeable tribal population, strategic border location, economic and infrastructural backwardness, and non-viable State finances. High per-capita income and commercially viable finances were not such parameters.

s: During which Five Year Plan was the Gadgil formula introduced in 1969 for distributing Central Plan assistance?
x: The Gadgil formula, associated with D. R. Gadgil, was introduced in 1969 during the Fourth Five Year Plan for distributing Central Plan assistance among States.

s: Why did the Gadgil and Gadgil-Mukherjee formulas lose their role in intergovernmental transfers?
o: The Planning Commission was abolished and Plan grants ended
The Fourteenth Finance Commission raised devolution to 42%
x: The formulas distributed Plan assistance; with the Planning Commission abolished and Plan grants ended, they lost their role.

s: From which Plan was the Gadgil-Mukherjee formula adopted in 1991?
x: The Gadgil-Mukherjee formula (1991) applied from the Eighth Plan; the Gadgil formula (1969) began with the Fourth Plan.

s: What weight did the Gadgil formula give to population?
x: Both the Gadgil and Gadgil-Mukherjee formulas gave population a weight of 60%.

s: Special category States traditionally received Central Plan assistance on which terms?
o: 100 percent grant without any loan component
x: Special category States had the first charge on Central Plan assistance and received it on the favourable terms of 90 percent grant and 10 percent loan.

s: What weight did the Gadgil-Mukherjee formula give to per-capita income?
x: Gadgil-Mukherjee (1991): population 60, per-capita income 25, performance 7.5, special problems 7.5.

s: What did the Article 131 suit in Kerala v. Union of India (2024) challenge?
o: The appointment of the Governor under Article 156
The distribution of river waters under Article 262
The Net Borrowing Ceiling imposed under Article 293(3)
The validity of GST under Article 279A
x: Kerala's 2024 suit under Article 131 challenged the Net Borrowing Ceiling imposed under Article 293(3).

s: Under Article 292, how may the Union Government borrow?
o: On the security of the Consolidated Fund of India, within limits fixed by Parliament by law
Only on the security of State Consolidated Funds
Only from foreign sources without parliamentary limits
Without reference to any law made by Parliament
x: Article 292 authorises Union borrowing on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India, subject to limits fixed by Parliament by law.

s: What power does Article 293(2) give, and to whom?
o: Supreme Court to fix the borrowing limit of every State
States to guarantee Union loans without limit
Union to lend to States or guarantee their loans
Finance Commission to sanction State loans
x: Article 293(2) empowers the Union to make loans to States and to guarantee loans raised by them.

s: Under Article 293(3), a State with an outstanding Union loan or guarantee needs what to raise a fresh loan?
o: Only the approval of the Reserve Bank of India
The Union's consent, which may carry conditions
No consent, if the loan is raised within India
x: While a Union loan or guarantee is outstanding, the State needs the Union's consent for a further loan, and conditions may be attached.

s: Under Article 293(1), how may a State borrow?
o: Within or outside India, on the security of its Consolidated Fund
Only outside India, with the Union's guarantee
Only within India, on the security of its Consolidated Fund
Within India, on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India
x: A State may borrow only within India on the security of its own Consolidated Fund; Article 293(1) does not allow direct foreign loans.

s: Through which Article is the Net Borrowing Ceiling on States, which counts off-budget borrowings, imposed?
x: The Net Borrowing Ceiling is imposed via Article 293(3), which requires Union consent for a State with an unpaid Union loan.

s: What were the net borrowings of Andhra Pradesh in 2024-25?
x: AP's net borrowings were Rs 60,485.40 crore in 2024-25.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the 80th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2000?
o: It gave effect to the Tenth Finance Commission's 'Alternative Scheme of Devolution'
It was made effective from 1 April 2000
It omitted Article 272 on sharing of Union excise duties
It made the States share the gross proceeds of all Union taxes
x: Though enacted in 2000, the 80th Amendment was made effective from 1 April 1996.

s: Which Constitutional Amendment omitted Article 272 on sharing of Union excise duties?
x: The 80th Amendment (2000) omitted Article 272 and made all central taxes shareable.

s: Which Constitutional Amendment inserted Article 268A on service tax?
x: Article 268A was added by the 88th Amendment (2003) and omitted by the 101st (2016).

s: From which date did the 80th Constitutional Amendment, enacted in 2000, take effect?
x: The 80th Amendment was enacted in 2000 but given effect from 1 April 1996.

s: Under the 80th Amendment scheme, what share of the gross proceeds of Union taxes went to the States for 1996-97 to 1999-2000?
x: The 80th Amendment, based on the 10th Finance Commission's Alternative Scheme of Devolution, gave States 29% of gross Union tax proceeds.

s: Which Constitutional Amendment raised the ceiling on profession tax from ₹250 to ₹2,500?
x: The Sixtieth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988 raised the profession-tax ceiling under Article 276 from ₹250 to ₹2,500 per annum.

s: Which of the following is a power of the Union during a Financial Emergency under Article 360?
o: To direct States on financial propriety and require Money Bills to be reserved for the President
To automatically assume all State legislative powers
x: During a Financial Emergency, the Centre may direct States on financial propriety and require Money and Financial Bills to be reserved for the President.

s: Which of the following is correct about Article 131 and the Finance Commission?
o: Article 131 abolishes the Finance Commission's advisory role
Every Finance Commission matter must be decided under Article 131
Article 131 applies only to disputes between private persons and States
Matters referred to the Finance Commission are excluded from Article 131
x: Matters referred to the Finance Commission are excluded from Article 131, which covers original Union-State and inter-State legal disputes.

s: Under which Article can the President modify the distribution of revenues between the Union and States during a National Emergency?
x: Article 354 allows this modification until the end of the financial year in which the emergency ends. Article 360 is Financial Emergency, 280 the Finance Commission and 293 State borrowing.

s: Until when does a modification of revenue distribution by the President under Article 354 last?
o: Financial year in which the emergency ends
x: Under Article 354, the modification lasts till the end of the financial year in which the National Emergency ends.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the IMDT Act?
o: It was upheld as strengthening the Union's duty under Article 355.
It was struck down in Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005).
The Supreme Court held that it violated Article 355.
x: The IMDT Act (1983) was struck down, not upheld, in Sarbananda Sonowal (2005) for violating Article 355.

s: Under Article 365, how may a State's failure to comply with Union directions be treated?
x: Article 365 treats defiance of Union directions as a breakdown of constitutional machinery, opening the way to Article 356.

s: What duty does Article 355 impose on the Union?
o: appoint State ministers during political instability
protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance
permit States to maintain their own armed forces
ensure every State follows the same economic policy
x: Article 355 requires the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and to ensure each State is governed according to the Constitution.

s: In which case was the IMDT Act, 1983 struck down for violating Article 355?
o: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India
Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005)
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
x: The Supreme Court struck down the IMDT Act in Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005) for violating Article 355.

s: Which of the following does Part XI of the Constitution deal with?
o: elections and special provisions for certain classes
legislative and administrative relations between the Union and the States
emergency provisions and amendment of the Constitution
financial relations and trade within India
x: Part XI contains legislative relations (Articles 245-255) and administrative relations (Articles 256-263) between the Union and the States.

s: Which of the following does Part XII of the Constitution primarily deal with?
o: Emergency relations between the Union and the States
Financial relations between the Union and the States
Administrative relations between the Union and the States
x: Part XII deals with financial relations, including Articles 268 to 293.

s: Which one of the following is a unitary feature of the Indian Constitution?
o: A constitutional prohibition on Union directions to States
Separate and independent judicial systems for the Union and each State
Dual citizenship for Union and State citizens
All India Services serving both the Union and the States
x: All India Services are a unitary feature because they provide a common administrative structure serving both the Union and the States. India has single citizenship and an integrated judiciary.

s: When was the Sarkaria Commission on Union-State relations formed?
x: The Sarkaria Commission, chaired by Justice R.S. Sarkaria, was formed on 9 June 1983.

s: Which Articles of the Constitution cover legislative relations between the Union and the States?
x: Part XI covers legislative relations in Articles 245-255 and administrative relations in Articles 256-263.

s:
Consider the following statements about the constitutional scheme of Centre-State relations:
1. Part XI covers legislative and administrative relations.
2. Part XII covers financial relations in Articles 268-293.
3. Administrative relations are dealt with in Part XII.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Administrative relations are in Part XI (Articles 256-263), so statement 3 is wrong.

s:
Which of the following has shaped Centre-State relations in India?
1. Constitutional provisions
2. Conventions and judicial interpretation
3. Planning and party politics
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Centre-State relations are shaped by constitutional provisions, conventions, judicial interpretation, planning and party politics.

s: Which of the following is NOT a unitary feature of the Indian Constitution?
o: Division of powers between the Union and the States
x: Single citizenship, an integrated judiciary, All India Services and emergency powers are unitary features; division of powers is a federal feature.

s: What does India's federal structure become during a National Emergency?
o: more strongly federal, with State powers protected
confederal, with States gaining international personality
unchanged in the legislative, executive and financial spheres
quasi-unitary, with increased powers for the Union
x: A National Emergency strengthens the Union, so the system operates in a unitary or quasi-unitary manner.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Emergency Articles:
1. Article 359 deals with the duty of the Union to protect the States.
2. Article 354 deals with the distribution of revenues during an Emergency.
3. Article 358 deals with the suspension of Article 19 during an Emergency.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Article 359 deals with suspension of enforcement of Fundamental Rights; the Union's duty to protect the States is Article 355.

s: What is the effect of Article 353 during a National Emergency?
o: State Governments are suspended and Parliament administers the States.
The Supreme Court assumes the executive functions of the States.
The Union may direct a State on any matter, but State Governments are not suspended.
The Governor alone exercises all executive power of the State.
x: Article 353 enlarges the Union's executive authority to direct a State on any matter; it does not suspend State Governments.

s: What may the President do under Article 354 during a National Emergency?
o: transfer all State taxes to the Consolidated Fund of India
suspend tax distribution without laying the order before Parliament
reduce or cancel certain transfers to States until the end of the financial year
x: Article 354 lets the President modify or reduce financial transfers to States, generally until the end of the financial year; the order must be laid before Parliament.

s: When do laws made by Parliament on State List matters under Article 250 cease to have effect?
o: One year after the Emergency ends
Only after repeal by every State Legislature
Six months after the Emergency ends
x: Such laws do not become void immediately; they cease to have effect six months after the National Emergency ends.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the effects of a National Emergency on Centre-State relations?
o: Laws made under Article 250 end six months after the Emergency ends
Cuts in transfers under Article 354 last till the end of that financial year
Under Article 353, State Governments are suspended
The Lok Sabha term can be extended by one year at a time
